core: A data type is a classification that tells the computer and programmer how to interpret a sequence of bits and which operations are valid on a value
Common primitive types: integer, floating-point, boolean, character/string
Type conversion: implicit (coercion) vs explicit (casting), with verified examples
Why types matter: memory layout, valid operations, and bug prevention (e.g., integer vs float division)
supporting: Composite/collection types named: array, list, tuple, set, dictionary/map
Static vs dynamic typing (when types are checked)
Strong vs weak typing (how strictly a language enforces type rules and coercion)
Floating-point values follow IEEE 754 and have finite precision
outOfScope: Operator precedence and full operator catalog (own topic)
Boolean truth tables / logic gates (own topic)
Deep treatment of arrays, lists, and dictionaries as data structures (own topics)

claims.claim: A data type classifies a value, telling the computer how to interpret its bits and which operations the value supports; in Python's model every object has a type, and the type determines the operations the object supports.
Common built-in types include integers (int), floating-point numbers (float), booleans (bool), and text strings (str); Python also provides collection types such as list, tuple, set, and dict.
In Python, bool is a subtype of int, and True and False behave like 1 and 0 in most numeric contexts (verified: True + True == 2, issubclass(bool, int) is True).

Explicit conversion (casting) uses an operation like int("42") to produce the integer 42; implicit conversion (coercion) happens automatically, e.g. 3 + 2.0 yields the float 5.0 (verified in python3).
Type choice changes results: in Python 3, 7 / 2 is the float 3.5 while 7 // 2 is the int 3 (verified in python3).

A language may be strongly typed (refuses to silently mix incompatible types) or weakly typed (coerces them). Python is strongly typed: "42" + 8 raises TypeError. JavaScript is weakly typed for +: 5 + "x" produces the string "5x" (both verified).

Floating-point numbers follow IEEE 754 (current edition 754-2019); the double-precision (binary64) format has finite precision, so values like 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 cannot all be stored exactly, and 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluates to False (verified in python3).
Static typing checks types before the program runs (at compile time); dynamic typing checks types while the program runs. These describe WHEN types are checked, a separate axis from strong vs weak.

sourceRecords.title: Built-in Types — Python 3 documentation
sourceRecords.notes: Authoritative list and semantics of int, float, complex, bool, str, list, tuple, set, dict. Confirms bool is a subclass of int and that True/False behave like 1/0 in numeric contexts. Used to support the primitive/collection type inventory and conversion behavior. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The Python Language Reference — Data model
sourceRecords.notes: States every object has an identity, a type, and a value, and that an object's type determines the operations it supports and its possible values. Supports the core definition that a type governs interpretation and permitted operations. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic (IEEE 754-2019)
sourceRecords.notes: Canonical standard for floating-point arithmetic; current edition 754-2019 defines binary64 (double precision) with finite precision. Canonical IEEE landing page recorded as the URL; the standard's facts (edition year, binary64, ~15-16 decimal digits, inexact decimals) were read from the public Wikipedia summary at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754 and cross-checked against verified python3 output (0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3). Used only to support the finite-precision claim.

sourceRecords.title: Addition (+) — JavaScript | MDN
sourceRecords.notes: Documents JavaScript's + operator coercing operands: if one side is a string the other is converted to a string and concatenated (e.g. 5 + "x" -> "5x"). Used as the weak-typing contrast against Python's strong typing. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
